en.statement: etcd stores the cluster state used by the Kubernetes API.
en.explanation: etcd is the consistent key-value store for Kubernetes API data, including workload objects.

en.statement: The cloud-controller-manager assigns unscheduled Pods to suitable Nodes.
en.explanation: kube-scheduler assigns unscheduled Pods to Nodes. cloud-controller-manager integrates the cluster with cloud provider APIs.

en.statement: The Job controller creates a Job's Pods by sending requests to kube-apiserver.
en.explanation: Controllers act through the API server: the Job controller creates or removes Pod objects, and the kubelet on each assigned Node runs their containers.

en.statement: A Deployment uses ReplicaSets to maintain the number of Pods it declares.
en.explanation: A Deployment manages Pods through ReplicaSets, which maintain its requested replica count.

en.statement: A StatefulSet assigns a fresh identity when it replaces a failed Pod.
en.explanation: A StatefulSet preserves each Pod's stable identity, including its ordinal and network identity, across replacement.

en.statement: A Job runs its Pods at intervals on a recurring schedule.
en.explanation: A CronJob creates Jobs on a repeating schedule; each Job runs a task toward completion.

en.statement: Deleting a Namespace leaves the Deployments and Services inside it running in the cluster.
en.explanation: Deleting a Namespace deletes everything in it, including its Deployments and Services. The deletion is asynchronous, so the Namespace shows Terminating for a while.

en.statement: Kubernetes uses annotation values to select groups of related objects.
en.explanation: Kubernetes uses labels to identify selectable groups of objects. Annotations carry metadata that selectors do not use.

en.statement: A regular init container finishes before the Pod's app containers start.
en.explanation: Regular init containers complete before app startup; native sidecars are the restartable form that continues running.

en.statement: A kubeconfig context combines a cluster, a user, and a Namespace.
en.explanation: A kubeconfig context groups those access settings; kubectl uses the current context for cluster requests.

source.title: Organizing Cluster Access Using kubeconfig Files

en.statement: Kubernetes serves Deployment objects through the core v1 API group.
en.explanation: Kubernetes serves Deployment objects through apps/v1, a named API group.

en.statement: kubectl apply keeps live-object changes from other writers in fields its file does not set.
en.explanation: kubectl apply patches only the differences it manages, so direct changes to live objects survive. The imperative kubectl replace overwrites the whole spec and drops them.

en.statement: A container's CPU request caps its CPU use while it runs.
en.explanation: A CPU request is a reservation, not a runtime ceiling. A container can use more CPU when capacity is available.

source.title: Resource Management for Pods and Containers

en.statement: A BestEffort Pod can have a CPU request on one of its containers.
en.explanation: BestEffort Pods have no CPU or memory requests or limits at container or Pod level. A CPU request changes the QoS class.

en.statement: Lowering a ResourceQuota below current usage leaves existing Pods in the Namespace running.
en.explanation: Quota is checked when objects are created or updated, so changing a ResourceQuota leaves existing resources alone. New requests that would exceed it are rejected.

en.statement: A LimitRange can supply default resource requests for new containers.
en.explanation: A LimitRange can fill in missing resource requests and limits for new containers in its Namespace.

en.statement: Creating a CustomResourceDefinition starts a controller that reconciles the custom resource.
en.explanation: A CustomResourceDefinition registers an API type but does not run its controller. The operator pattern combines custom resources with a separate controller.

en.statement: Running a kubeadm control plane upgrade upgrades the cluster's worker nodes as part of it.
en.explanation: A kubeadm cluster upgrade has separate control plane and worker node stages. Workers are upgraded after the control plane.

en.statement: kube-scheduler uses a Pod's resource requests when filtering candidate Nodes.
en.explanation: The scheduler checks whether a Node has enough unrequested capacity for the Pod's resource requests.

en.statement: A Pod's nodeSelector restricts placement to Nodes with matching labels.
en.explanation: nodeSelector makes matching Node labels a placement condition for the Pod.

en.statement: A running Pod is evicted once its Node loses a label its required node affinity matched.
en.explanation: Node affinity is checked at scheduling time. If the Node's labels change after placement, the Pod keeps running; that is what IgnoredDuringExecution in the rule types means.

en.statement: Inter-pod affinity compares labels on Pods already running in a topology domain.
en.explanation: Inter-pod affinity uses labels of existing Pods within a topology domain to steer placement of a new Pod.

en.statement: A matching toleration guarantees that a Pod lands on its tainted Node.
en.explanation: A toleration permits placement on a tainted Node but does not direct the Pod there; other scheduling rules still apply.

en.statement: A pending Pod can preempt running Pods whose priority equals its own.
en.explanation: When a pending Pod cannot be scheduled, the scheduler tries to evict Pods of lower priority than it. Pods of equal or higher priority are left in place.

en.statement: A zone-based topology spread rule calculates skew from Pod counts on individual Nodes.
en.explanation: Topology spread measures skew across topology domains. With a zone key, it compares zones rather than individual Nodes.

en.statement: kube-scheduler moves a Pod that no Node can accept into the Failed phase.
en.explanation: Such a Pod stays in the Pending phase, which covers the time a Pod spends waiting to be scheduled, until a Node can take it.

en.statement: kubectl cordon leaves existing Pods on the marked Node in place.
en.explanation: kubectl cordon marks a Node unschedulable for ordinary new placements but does not evict its existing Pods.

en.statement: Process-isolated Linux containers on one Node share the Node's kernel.
en.explanation: Containers are processes running on a shared kernel, while a virtual machine runs its own kernel, which gives the VM a stronger isolation boundary.

en.statement: Linux cgroups constrain the CPU and memory available to containers.
en.explanation: cgroups let the Linux kernel constrain resources allocated to container processes.

en.statement: A running container writes file changes into its original image layers.
en.explanation: Container images provide read-only layers. A running container records filesystem changes in a separate writable layer.

en.statement: Pinning a container image by tag gives the same content guarantee as pinning it by digest.
en.explanation: Tags can be moved to point to different images. A digest is a hash of the image content and stays fixed, so image@sha256:... pins one exact version.

en.statement: A Pod whose RuntimeClass names a hardware-virtualized runtime handler runs under it while other Pods keep the default.
en.explanation: Each RuntimeClass names a handler, a runtime configuration on the nodes, so workloads that need stronger isolation trade some overhead for a VM-based runtime.

en.statement: With the Always image pull policy, the runtime downloads cached layers again.
en.explanation: The Always policy makes the runtime check the registry at launch; it reuses image layers already cached locally.

en.statement: The OCI Image Specification defines the registry API that clients use to push and pull images.
en.explanation: The OCI Distribution Specification standardizes the API for distributing images. The Image Specification defines the image, with enough information to launch it.

en.statement: The Container Runtime Interface carries requests from kubelet to a runtime.
en.explanation: The Container Runtime Interface is the protocol between the kubelet and a compatible container runtime.

en.statement: The kubelet uses runc as its Container Runtime Interface endpoint.
en.explanation: runc is a low-level OCI runtime called by higher-level runtimes such as containerd or CRI-O; it is not the kubelet's CRI endpoint.

en.statement: Pods on the cluster Pod network receive distinct IP addresses across the cluster.
en.explanation: The Kubernetes network model gives Pods on the cluster network unique IP addresses, including when they run on different Nodes.

en.statement: On each Node, the container runtime loads the CNI plugins that implement the Kubernetes Pod network.
en.explanation: The container runtime on each Node, such as containerd or CRI-O, is configured to load the CNI plugins required to implement the Kubernetes network model.

en.statement: Kubernetes creates a Service as type ClusterIP when its manifest leaves the type field unset.
en.explanation: ClusterIP is the default Service type: its virtual IP is reachable only from inside the cluster. Exposing it outside takes another type, an Ingress or a Gateway.

en.statement: Under the default external traffic policy, a NodePort Service needs a backend Pod on the contacted Node.
en.explanation: The default Cluster policy routes NodePort traffic to ready endpoints on any Node. Only the Local policy delivers to node-local endpoints and drops traffic at Nodes with none.

en.statement: An ExternalName Service answers DNS lookups with a CNAME for its target hostname.
en.explanation: Cluster DNS returns a CNAME pointing to the configured hostname. Kubernetes does not proxy traffic for an ExternalName Service.

en.statement: A headless Service can use kube-proxy to distribute traffic across backend Pods.
en.explanation: kube-proxy does not handle headless Services. Cluster DNS supplies backend addresses so clients can connect to them directly.

en.statement: An HTTPRoute creates the listener that receives traffic for a Gateway.
en.explanation: A Gateway defines listeners and traffic-handling infrastructure. An attached HTTPRoute defines rules for sending HTTP requests to backends.

en.statement: NetworkPolicy rules depend on a network plugin that enforces them.
en.explanation: The NetworkPolicy API object alone does not filter packets. A compatible network plugin must implement its rules.

en.statement: A service mesh routes application traffic through its control plane to enforce policy.
en.explanation: Data plane proxies handle application traffic and enforce policy. The service mesh control plane configures those proxies outside the traffic path.

en.statement: Admission control can examine an API request before the authorization stage.
en.explanation: The API server runs authorization before admission control. Admission controllers then inspect, modify or reject applicable requests.

source.title: Controlling Access to the Kubernetes API

en.statement: An RBAC Role grants permissions within one Namespace.
en.explanation: An RBAC Role contains rules scoped to the Namespace where it exists. Those rules do not grant access in other Namespaces.

en.statement: A RoleBinding grants a referenced ClusterRole across the whole cluster.
en.explanation: A RoleBinding remains scoped to its Namespace even when it references a ClusterRole. A ClusterRoleBinding grants access across the cluster.

en.statement: The kubelet refreshes a Pod's projected ServiceAccount token before the token expires.
en.explanation: The kubelet fetches time-bound, Pod-bound tokens through the TokenRequest API and mounts them in a projected volume, replacing the older Secret-based tokens that never expired.

en.statement: A Secret's data entries are base64-encoded in its API representation.
en.explanation: Values in a Secret's data field use base64 encoding. The stringData field offers a way to supply plain strings when creating a Secret.

en.statement: The API server encrypts Secret data in etcd by default.
en.explanation: The default API server configuration stores Secrets in etcd without at-rest encryption. Cluster operators can configure encryption for them.

en.statement: The Baseline Pod Security Standard forbids containers that run as the root user.
en.explanation: Baseline blocks known privilege escalations and allows a minimally specified Pod. Requiring containers to run as non-root users is a control of the Restricted standard.

en.statement: A container security context overrides a Pod security context for shared settings.
en.explanation: When the same security setting exists at both levels, the container's setting takes precedence for that container.

source.title: Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container

en.statement: The Distribute security phase controls which workloads a user may deploy.
en.explanation: The Distribute phase focuses on the software supply chain, including container images. Restrictions on what and who may deploy belong to the Deploy phase.

en.statement: A Pod in Running phase has passed the readiness checks configured for its containers.
en.explanation: Running means the Pod is bound to a Node and its containers have been created. Readiness is tracked separately and can still be false.

en.statement: After repeated image pull failures, the kubelet gives up on the image until the Pod is recreated.
en.explanation: With ImagePullBackOff the container stays Waiting while Kubernetes keeps retrying the pull, raising the back-off delay between attempts up to a limit.

en.statement: With the Always restart policy, the kubelet restarts a container that was OOMKilled.
en.explanation: OOMKilled is the termination reason for a container that kept using memory beyond its limit. If the container can be restarted, the kubelet restarts it as after any runtime failure, so the kill can repeat.

source.title: Assign Memory Resources to Containers and Pods

en.statement: Kubernetes Events form a durable history of changes to cluster objects.
en.explanation: Events are best-effort reports of activity or state changes and have limited retention. They are not a durable audit log.

en.statement: The node controller marks a Node Ready condition Unknown after losing contact.
en.explanation: When a Node becomes unreachable, the node controller changes its Ready condition to Unknown. Continued unreachability can lead to Pod eviction.

en.statement: A failed liveness probe replaces the whole Pod with a newly scheduled Pod.
en.explanation: After enough liveness failures, the kubelet restarts the affected container inside its existing Pod. Replacing the Pod is not the direct probe action.

en.statement: The kubelet leaves a container running when its readiness probe fails.
en.explanation: A failed readiness probe makes the container unready while the kubelet keeps it running and continues probing.

en.statement: A startup probe delays liveness and readiness checks until it succeeds.
en.explanation: When a startup probe is configured, the kubelet waits for it to succeed before running liveness or readiness probes.

en.statement: Cluster DNS stops resolving a ClusterIP Service's name once its selector stops matching any ready Pod.
en.explanation: The Kubernetes DNS specification keeps an A record mapping a ClusterIP Service's name to its cluster IP whatever its endpoints. Only headless Service records follow ready endpoints.

en.statement: A container restart recreates the Pod's ephemeral volumes.
en.explanation: For any kind of volume in a Pod, data is preserved across container restarts. Kubernetes destroys ephemeral volumes such as emptyDir when the Pod itself ceases to exist.

en.statement: A ConfigMap volume exposes configuration entries as files inside a container.
en.explanation: A mounted ConfigMap volume presents its selected entries as files at the container's mount path.

en.statement: Kubernetes stores a PersistentVolume in the Namespace of its bound PersistentVolumeClaim.
en.explanation: A PersistentVolume is a cluster-wide resource. Its bound PersistentVolumeClaim is namespaced.

en.statement: A PersistentVolume larger than a claim's request is eligible to bind to that claim.
en.explanation: Kubernetes guarantees a claim at least the capacity it asked for. When it binds to an existing PersistentVolume, that volume may be larger than the request.

en.statement: A StorageClass creates storage before any PersistentVolumeClaim requests it.
en.explanation: A StorageClass describes how a provisioner creates storage. Dynamic provisioning responds to a matching PersistentVolumeClaim, rather than creation of the class.

en.statement: ReadWriteOnce restricts a volume to one Pod, even when several Pods share a Node.
en.explanation: ReadWriteOnce limits read-write mounting to one Node, which may run multiple Pods using that volume. ReadWriteOncePod provides single-Pod access.

en.statement: A released Retain PersistentVolume stays unbindable until an administrator reclaims it.
en.explanation: After its claim is deleted, a Retain volume is Released but keeps the previous claimant's data, so no claim can bind it. An administrator reclaims the storage manually, deleting and recreating the PersistentVolume.

en.statement: Storage vendors ship their CSI drivers outside the Kubernetes repository.
en.explanation: CSI is an out-of-tree plugin interface, so vendors build storage plugins without adding source code to Kubernetes. An out-of-tree CSI driver is the recommended way to integrate external storage.

en.statement: A StatefulSet's volumeClaimTemplate gives its replicas one PersistentVolumeClaim to share.
en.explanation: For each volumeClaimTemplate entry, a StatefulSet gives every Pod its own PersistentVolumeClaim, so each replica keeps separate, stable storage.

en.statement: A Deployment's RollingUpdate strategy can bound extra and unavailable Pods during replacement.
en.explanation: RollingUpdate uses separate bounds for extra Pods and unavailable Pods, letting a Deployment replace replicas gradually.

en.statement: A Deployment's Recreate strategy starts replacement Pods before removing the old Pods.
en.explanation: During a Recreate upgrade, the Deployment terminates the old revision's Pods before creating Pods for the new revision.

en.statement: Rolling a Deployment back to an earlier revision restores the replica count it had at that revision.
en.explanation: Scaling creates no Deployment revision, so a rollback restores only the Pod template and the Deployment keeps its current replica count.

en.statement: Argo Rollouts scales down the old ReplicaSet in a blue-green update before it switches the active Service.
en.explanation: The controller points the active Service at the new ReplicaSet first and scales the old one down only after scaleDownDelaySeconds, giving every Node time to update its IP tables.

en.statement: A canary rollout sends a small share of live traffic to a new version beside the stable version.
en.explanation: A canary introduces the new version to part of the live traffic while the stable version continues serving the rest.

en.statement: Installing the same Helm chart twice in one cluster produces two separate releases.
en.explanation: A Helm release is an instance of a chart running in a cluster. Each installation gets its own release name, so one chart can run several times side by side.

en.statement: A Kustomize overlay can edit base resource files in place to create an environment variant.
en.explanation: A Kustomize overlay applies changes on top of a reusable base. It does not need to modify the base files, which can serve other overlays.

source.title: Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Kustomize

en.statement: In OpenGitOps, a saved desired-state revision may be edited after deployment.
en.explanation: OpenGitOps calls for desired state to be stored with immutable revisions, versioning, and a complete history.

en.statement: Argo CD continuously compares an application's live Kubernetes state with the target state declared in Git.
en.explanation: Argo CD runs as a Kubernetes controller. When live state deviates from the Git target, it marks the application OutOfSync and syncs it back automatically or on request.

source.title: Argo CD - Declarative GitOps CD for Kubernetes

en.statement: kubectl logs takes a container name to print just that container's output from a multi-container Pod.
en.explanation: With a container name, kubectl logs reads one container of a multi-container Pod, so its output focuses on the container under investigation.

en.statement: kubectl logs shows a restarted container's previous instance by default.
en.explanation: kubectl logs normally reads the current container instance. The previous instance's logs need an explicit selection.

en.statement: kubectl describe includes Events associated with the resource being inspected.
en.explanation: kubectl describe presents resource details together with related Events, which can reveal scheduling or runtime problems.

en.statement: kubectl get events lists Event resources in the current Namespace by default.
en.explanation: Events are namespaced resources. kubectl get events uses the current Namespace unless another Namespace or all Namespaces are requested.

en.statement: kubectl exec starts a diagnostic command in a newly created Pod.
en.explanation: kubectl exec runs a command inside a container of an existing Pod. It does not create a diagnostic Pod.

en.statement: kubectl port-forward to a Service load-balances connections across the Service's ready Pods.
en.explanation: kubectl port-forward picks one Pod behind the target and sends all forwarded traffic to it. If that Pod terminates, the session ends and the command must be run again.

en.statement: kubectl debug can add an ephemeral diagnostic container to an existing Pod.
en.explanation: An ephemeral container lets an operator bring debugging tools into a running Pod whose application image lacks them.

en.statement: By default, kubectl rollout status keeps watching a Deployment rollout until the latest revision is done.
en.explanation: It reports progress until the rollout finishes. If a newer rollout starts while it waits, it continues watching that latest revision instead.

en.statement: kubectl rollout history lists previous container restarts for a Deployment.
en.explanation: kubectl rollout history shows a Deployment's rollout revisions and their recorded configurations, not individual container restarts.

en.statement: In Prometheus's primary collection model, monitored targets push samples to the Prometheus server.
en.explanation: Prometheus primarily collects metrics by scraping configured targets. Regular targets expose samples for Prometheus to fetch.

en.statement: On a Prometheus metric, each distinct value of a user ID label produces a separate time series.
en.explanation: Every unique combination of label values is a separate series, so unbounded labels such as user IDs sharply increase the data Prometheus stores.

en.statement: PromQL can evaluate log entries alongside metric samples in a Prometheus query.
en.explanation: PromQL queries Prometheus time series. It does not treat raw log entries as another input to a metrics expression.

en.statement: Prometheus servers evaluate alerting rules and send the firing alerts to Alertmanager.
en.explanation: Alerting is split in two: Prometheus servers evaluate the rules, then Alertmanager handles silencing, inhibition, aggregation and notifications by email, on-call systems or chat.

en.statement: Library calls to the OpenTelemetry API emit telemetry once the application imports an SDK.
en.explanation: A library can depend on the OpenTelemetry API alone, which has no effect on the application until the application imports the SDK that processes and exports telemetry.

en.statement: The OpenTelemetry Collector stores traces as the system of record for later queries.
en.explanation: The OpenTelemetry Collector receives, processes, and exports telemetry to backends. It is a pipeline component, not a queryable trace store.

en.statement: Kubernetes can write container stdout and stderr to a built-in cluster-wide log store.
en.explanation: Kubernetes captures container output through node-level logging, but it provides no built-in cluster-wide log storage.

en.statement: The Metrics API supplies CPU and memory usage to Kubernetes autoscalers.
en.explanation: The Metrics API exposes basic Pod and Node resource usage for autoscaling. A metrics-server or another implementation serves the API.

en.statement: An SLO is the raw measurement collected for a service's reliability target.
en.explanation: An SLI measures service behavior. An SLO states the reliability objective associated with one or more SLIs.

en.statement: CNCF's cloud native model confines application deployment to public cloud providers.
en.explanation: CNCF describes cloud native technologies as usable in public, private, and hybrid clouds.

en.statement: Splitting an application into microservices lowers the operational overhead of running it.
en.explanation: Microservices ease independent deployment and scaling, but they add operational overhead: the things a team must deploy and keep track of grow by an order of magnitude.

en.statement: A HorizontalPodAutoscaler scales a StatefulSet by changing its replica count.
en.explanation: A HorizontalPodAutoscaler updates the replicas of a scalable workload resource such as a Deployment or StatefulSet. Objects that cannot be scaled, like a DaemonSet, are outside it.

en.statement: A VerticalPodAutoscaler adjusts Pod resource requests based on usage patterns.
en.explanation: A VerticalPodAutoscaler analyzes resource usage and recommends updated CPU or memory requests for targeted Pods.

en.statement: When Pods are pending for lack of capacity, Cluster Autoscaler sets up extra Node groups to hold them.
en.explanation: Cluster Autoscaler adds Nodes to Node groups that were preconfigured; the Node groups it can provision from have to exist already.

en.statement: Knative Serving can scale service Pods to zero after traffic stops.
en.explanation: Knative Serving supports scaling idle services down to zero Pods and scaling them up when requests return.

en.statement: A Kubernetes cluster can pair a CRI runtime, CNI network plugin, and CSI driver from separate vendors.
en.explanation: CRI, CNI, and CSI define interfaces for runtimes, networking, and storage, allowing compatible implementations to be selected independently.

en.statement: The CNCF Landscape treats an entry as a CNCF-hosted project once it appears on the map.
en.explanation: The CNCF Landscape catalogs cloud native projects and products beyond CNCF-hosted projects. An entry does not grant project membership.

en.statement: The CNCF operates as part of the Linux Foundation.
en.explanation: The Cloud Native Computing Foundation is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation, which hosts open source communities.

en.statement: The CNCF Governing Board maintains technical roadmaps for hosted projects.
en.explanation: The CNCF Governing Board handles marketing, business oversight, and budget decisions. Project technical direction belongs to the technical community.

en.statement: The CNCF Technical Oversight Committee admits projects into CNCF.
en.explanation: The Technical Oversight Committee evaluates and accepts projects into CNCF as part of its technical governance role.

en.statement: TAG Observability is among CNCF's active Technical Advisory Groups.
en.explanation: CNCF's current TAG roster places observability within TAG Operational Resilience; TAG Observability is a former group name.

en.statement: A CNCF project whose maintainers come from one company can graduate.
en.explanation: CNCF graduation criteria ask for project maintainers from at least two organizations, which shows the project can survive the loss of any single company.

en.statement: Kubernetes working groups disband once they reach the goals they were formed to deliver.
en.explanation: Working groups are temporary, own no code and form around a clear deliverable; they are disbanded after reaching their stated goals.

en.statement: A KEP records a release announcement after a Kubernetes feature ships.
en.explanation: A Kubernetes Enhancement Proposal communicates and coordinates a proposed change before the work is completed.

en.statement: The Kubernetes Release Team coordinates release work within SIG Release.
en.explanation: The Release Team sits within SIG Release and handles the day-to-day work needed to produce Kubernetes releases.

en.statement: Kubernetes wrote its own code of conduct, separate from the CNCF Code of Conduct.
en.explanation: Kubernetes follows the CNCF Code of Conduct. Its own Code of Conduct Committee handles incidents in the Kubernetes community.
